title: Input Validation, Output Encoding & Secret Management
objectives: Validate at every trust boundary with allowlists over blocklists
Normalize before validating so encodings cannot smuggle payload
Apply context-specific output encoding on the way out
Store and rotate secrets so a repo leak is not an incident
body:
Secure inputs and outputs are two halves of one habit. Inputs arrive at trust boundaries — HTTP handlers, webhooks, file uploads, env vars — and must be checked against what you *expect* (allowlists), after normalization. Outputs leave into hostile contexts — HTML, SQL, URLs — and must be encoded for the destination. Secrets are the third rail: they must exist outside the repo and die on schedule.

## The problem
A username field is 'protected' by a blocklist of banned words, an email is validated with a 400-line regex copied from a forum, and the database password lives in a file committed 'temporarily' two years ago. Each is a different failure of the same discipline: define what is valid, check after normalizing, and keep secrets out of anything that gets committed.

## Constraints
- Blocklists always lag: you ban `<script>` and attackers respond with encodings, Unicode confusables or split payloads.
- Validation must run after canonicalization (decode, trim, normalize case/encoding) or the check validates a different string than the one later used.
- Encoding is context-specific on output: HTML body, attribute, JS string, URL, SQL each need their own mechanism (recap of the XSS lesson).
- A secret in git history is compromised forever — deletion of the file is not rotation.
- Secure defaults mean new features start restricted and are loosened deliberately, never the reverse.

## Options
```js
// Allowlist: describe what IS valid, reject everything else
function validUsername(raw) {
  const s = raw.trim().toLowerCase()        // normalize first
  return /^[a-z0-9_]{3,20}$/.test(s) ? s : null
}

// Schema validation for structured input (shape, types, ranges)
const Body = z.object({
  email: z.string().email(),
  age: z.number().int().min(0).max(130)
})
const body = Body.safeParse(req.body)       // reject with 400 on failure

// Secrets: injected at runtime, scoped, rotated
const key = process.env.PAYMENTS_API_KEY    // never a literal, never in git
```

The allowlist pattern is deliberately boring: three character classes, length bounds, normalized — and entire CVE classes are unreachable.

## Tradeoffs
Allowlists refuse legitimate-but-unusual input (names with apostrophes, international characters) until you widen the pattern thoughtfully — that friction is the price of precision. Centralized schema validation adds a library and per-endpoint schemas, and buys one consistent rejection path with good errors. Secret managers (Vault, cloud KMS/Secrets Manager) add operational surface and eliminate the rotate-after-leak scramble.

## Decision
Normalize, then validate with allowlists or schemas at every boundary; reject loudly and log. Encode at output for the exact destination context. Keep secrets in environment or secret-manager storage, scoped per service and per environment, rotated on a schedule — and assume anything that ever touched git is burned.

## Measure it
Fuzz your own boundaries in CI: run the test suite with mutated inputs (overlong, encoded, type-swapped) and assert every endpoint rejects with 4xx and a log line. Scan the repo and history for secret patterns (trufflehog/gitleaks) on every push. Track validation-rejection rates per endpoint — a sudden drop can mean a new route skipped validation.

## Best practices
- Validate at every trust boundary; nothing internal is 'probably safe'.
- Prefer allowlists and schemas over blocklists; normalize before checking.
- Encode output per context; never build markup, queries or commands from strings.
- Keep secrets in env/secret-manager, scoped per environment, rotated regularly.
- Default secure: restrictions on first, explicit relaxation with review.

## Common mistakes
- Validating client-side only, or trusting a hidden field as validation.
- Blocklisting known-bad strings and losing to the next encoding trick.
- Checking length before trimming, or validating before decoding — the check tests a different value than the one used.
- Committing a .env file, then deleting it and calling it fixed without rotation.
- Reusing production secrets in staging, so one leaked environment compromises both.

## Production considerations
- Run secret scanning in CI on every push; treat a hit as an incident: rotate first, clean history second.
- Give each service its own credentials so blast radius is one service, not the platform.
- Centralize validation and rejection logging so coverage is auditable per endpoint.
- Schedule rotation for long-lived credentials (DB, API keys) and rehearse it — rotation you have never run is rotation that fails during an incident.

examples.name: validate-and-secrets.js

exercise.prompt: Implement the username allowlist validator: normalize (trim + lowercase), then accept only a-z, 0-9 and underscore, length 3–20 after normalization. Render pass/fail plus the normalized value for each sample, including trick inputs: leading/trailing spaces, uppercase, too long, and a blocklist-style 'bad<script>' which must fail simply because of invalid characters. The starter accepts everything.
hints: Normalize first: trim and lowercase, then validate the normalized value.
The allowlist is ^[a-z0-9_]{3,20}$ — anything else fails, no banned-word list needed.
GRACE-99 must fail on the hyphen; bad<script> fails on invalid chars, not on a blocklist.

questions.prompt: Why are allowlists preferred over blocklists for input validation?
options: Blocklists must enumerate every bad input forever, while allowlists reject anything not explicitly expected
questions.explanation: Blocklists play whack-a-mole with encodings and novel payloads; an allowlist defines the valid universe and everything else is rejected by construction.

questions.prompt: A secret was accidentally committed and the file was deleted in the next commit. What is the correct response?
options: Nothing else needed — the file is gone from HEAD
Rotate the secret immediately; git history still contains it
Re-run the CI pipeline to purge history automatically
questions.explanation: Deletion from the working tree does not touch history; anything committed must be treated as compromised and rotated before any history cleanup.
